title: Unit 3 test: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions
author: bc-tests-foundation
directions: This original practice test reports raw points only. Work without a calculator in Section I Part A and Section II Part B. A graphing calculator is allowed in the other parts. Angles are in radians. Give exact answers without a calculator and numerical answers to three decimal places when needed. Show mathematical reasoning on every free-response part.

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: Choose one answer for each question. No calculator is allowed.

items.prompt: If f(x) = ln(1 + x^4), what is f′(1)?
items.rationale: The chain rule gives f′(x) = 4x^3/(1 + x^4), which equals 2 at x = 1.

distractorNotes.A: Differentiates the logarithm but omits the inner derivative.
distractorNotes.C: Multiplies by 1 + x^4 instead of dividing by it.

items.prompt: The curve x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7 passes through (1, 2). What is dy/dx at this point?
items.rationale: Differentiation gives 2x + y + x y′ + 2y y′ = 0, so y′ = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y) = −4/5.

distractorNotes.A: Takes the reciprocal of the required slope.
distractorNotes.C: Uses −y/x instead of implicitly differentiating the curve equation.
distractorNotes.D: Loses the negative sign when isolating dy/dx.

items.prompt: A differentiable one-to-one function f satisfies f(2) = 5 and f′(2) = −3. If g is its differentiable inverse, what is g′(5)?
items.rationale: Differentiate f(g(y)) = y: f′(g(y))g′(y) = 1. At y = 5, g(5) = 2, giving g′(5) = −1/3.

distractorNotes.B: Takes the reciprocal of an output value rather than a derivative.
distractorNotes.D: Uses the slope of f rather than the reciprocal slope of its inverse.

items.prompt: If f(x) = arctan(2x), what is f′(1/2)?
items.rationale: The derivative is 2/(1 + 4x^2); substitution of x = 1/2 gives 2/2.

distractorNotes.B: Omits the factor 2 from the inner derivative.
distractorNotes.D: Uses the mistaken formula 1/(1 − x^2), both choosing the wrong inverse-trigonometric formula and omitting the inner factor 2.

items.prompt: If f(x) = x^2 e^x, what is f″(0)?
items.rationale: Twice applying the product rule gives f″(x) = (x^2 + 4x + 2)e^x; at zero only 2 remains.

distractorNotes.A: The constant term after two differentiations is 2, not 4; every remaining term contains x and vanishes at zero.
distractorNotes.B: Differentiates x^2e^x as though its zero factor persists through two derivatives.
distractorNotes.D: Omits the coefficient 2 from differentiating x^2 twice.

items.prompt: Which expression equals the derivative of y = ln((x^2 + 1)^3) for all real x?
items.rationale: Simplify to y = 3 ln(x^2 + 1), then differentiate to obtain 6x/(x^2 + 1). A nested chain rule gives the same result.

distractorNotes.A: Differentiates the inner cube but omits the outer logarithm derivative.
distractorNotes.B: Omits the factor 3 from the logarithm of a cube.
distractorNotes.C: Omits the derivative 2x after using the logarithm power rule.

items.prompt:
The table gives exact values for differentiable functions f and g. For H(x) = f(g(x)), what is H′(1)?
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 2 | 5 | 4 | −2
4 | 7 | 3 | 1 | 6

distractorNotes.A: Uses f′(1) rather than f′(g(1)) = f′(4).
distractorNotes.C: Uses only the outer derivative and omits g′(1).

items.prompt: A positive differentiable function y satisfies y^2 = x + 3 near (1, 2). What is y″ at (1, 2)?
items.rationale: From 2y y′ = 1, y′ = 1/4. Differentiating again gives 2(y′)^2 + 2y y″ = 0, hence y″ = −(1/16)/2.

distractorNotes.B: Drops the negative sign in y″ = −(y′)^2/y.
distractorNotes.D: Omits division by y in the second implicit derivative.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Choose one answer for each question. A graphing calculator is needed for some numerical work.

items.prompt: For f(x) = e^(−x) sin(x^2), what is f′(0.8) to three decimal places?
items.rationale: Product and chain rules give f′(x) = e^(−x)[2x cos(x^2) − sin(x^2)], which at 0.8 is 0.308.

distractorNotes.B: Omits the factor 2x from differentiating sin(x^2).
distractorNotes.C: Uses a positive sign for the derivative of e^(−x).
distractorNotes.D: Keeps the differentiated sine term but omits the differentiated exponential term.

items.prompt: Let f(x) = x + e^x, and let g be its inverse. Which number best approximates g′(3)?
items.rationale: Solve a + e^a = 3, obtaining a ≈ 0.792. Then g′(3) = 1/(1 + e^a) ≈ 0.312.

distractorNotes.A: Uses 1/f′(3) instead of evaluating f′ at the preimage of 3.
distractorNotes.B: Uses the original function slope at the preimage without taking its reciprocal.
distractorNotes.D: Reports the preimage g(3), not its derivative.

items.prompt: For f(x) = arcsin(x/3), what is f′(1.2) to three decimal places?
items.rationale: The derivative (1/3)/√(1 − x^2/9) simplifies to 1/√(9 − x^2), giving 0.364.

distractorNotes.A: Uses 9 + x^2 inside the square root, confusing inverse-trigonometric formulas.
distractorNotes.C: Uses 9 − x^2 instead of its square root in the denominator.

items.prompt: If f(x) = ln(1 + x^2), what is f″(1.7) to three decimal places?
items.rationale: First f′(x) = 2x/(1 + x^2). The quotient rule gives f″(x) = 2(1 − x^2)/(1 + x^2)^2, hence −0.250.

distractorNotes.A: Differentiates only the numerator of f′ and keeps the denominator fixed.
distractorNotes.C: Reverses the subtraction in the quotient-rule numerator.
distractorNotes.D: Reports f′(1.7) instead of the second derivative.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Show the equations used for numerical results and include units where appropriate.

items.prompt: A calibration assigns a reading r = F(x) = x + ln x to each positive input x. Both x and r are dimensionless. Since F is strictly increasing with range all real numbers, it has an inverse G.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find a = G(2.6), and write the equation you solve.
steps: G(2.6) is the positive input for which F(a) = 2.6.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find G′(2.6), using your value of a. Explain the reciprocal derivative relationship.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates the inverse identity using the chain rule.

steps: Differentiate F(G(r)) = r to get F′(G(r))G′(r) = 1.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Differentiate the identity from part (b) again to find G″(2.6). Show how both chain-rule factors enter.

rubric.criterion: Isolates G″ with the cube of F′ in the denominator.

steps: The differentiated identity is F″(G(r))(G′(r))^2 + F′(G(r))G″(r) = 0.
Substitute G′ = 1/F′ and solve for G″.

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: Show your reasoning and give exact answers. No calculator is allowed.

items.prompt: Consider the ellipse x^2 + 4y^2 = 20 near the point (2, 2), where the upper branch defines y as a differentiable function of x.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find dy/dx at (2, 2) and write an equation of the tangent line there.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates implicitly with the factor y′.

steps: Use the point and slope in the line equation.

rubric.criterion: Includes both (y′)^2 and y y″ when differentiating the product.
Substitutes the correct point and first derivative.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Near (2, 2), the same branch can also be written as x = g(y). Find g′(2) and justify its relationship to your answer in part (a).

rubric.criterion: Recognizes the local inverse relationship or differentiates with respect to y.
Correctly uses the nonzero original slope or the differentiated equation.
Obtains −4 and identifies it as the reciprocal slope.

steps: Locally the two function descriptions are inverses.
